newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: FRESH CLASHES IN BANGUI.
newsitem.headline: FRESH CLASHES IN BANGUI.

text.p: Fresh clashes between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers broke out in the capital of the Central African Republic on Saturday, one day after a clash which killed a peacekeeper and a child, witnesses said.
A spokesman for the African force, deployed to help restore peace after three army mutinies in under a year, said fresh clashes had broken out on Saturday morning.
Witnesses said Saturday's clash pitted Senegalese and Chadian peacekeepers against disaffected soldiers and spoke of civilians being wounded by stray bullets.

The African force, deployed under a January 25 peace deal, has been touted as a model for a force to restore peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic where similar ethnic and political clashes broke out on June 5.
Saturday's clashes focused on suburbs where the dissident soldiers, principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, enjoy popular support.
A spokesman for the soldiers, many of whom have already rejoined their units under the deal, said earlier they had told their men not to attack but to remain on the defensive.
A spokesman for the peacekeepers told of contacts between the two sides but said no formal meeting had been organised.
The Red Cross said the soldier was shot dead in Friday's clashes and a boy aged 12 had been killed by an explosion. He said eight other people had been wounded, one seriously.
Friday's incident was the first since a failed June 13 attempt to reintegrate mutineers from the paramilitary gendarmerie into their units under the January peace plan.
Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the January deal, was expected back in Bangui on Saturday.

The first mutinies, in April and May 1996, began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Peacekeepers' spokesman Captain Lamine Gueye said Friday's shooting erupted when peacekeepers intervened to stop a group of former mutineers holding up a private vehicle.
But Parfait Mbaye, a spokesman for the disaffected troops, said there had been no attempted hold-up and the peacekeepers had tried to disarm former mutineers returning to their base.
The trigger for Saturday's clash was not immediately clear.

French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order after the latest mutiny and handed over to the peacekeepers. The African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
